In July 1776, about a week after the colonies declared independence, John Dickinson of Pennsylvania presented Congress with a plan for a national government. Many delegates objected that it gave Congress too much power. They had just declared war on a king, and most Americans felt loyal first to their own state.

A League of Friendship

Congress spent more than a year cutting the plan down. Thomas Burke of North Carolina proposed the rule that became Article II, which said that "each state retains its sovereignty, freedom, and independence." In November 1777, Congress approved the Articles of Confederation, the first written plan of government for the United States. The plan created a confederation, a loose union of independent states that work together for a common purpose, and it described that union as "a firm league of friendship." There was no president and no system of national courts, and each state had one vote regardless of its population. The states finished approving the plan in 1781.

The Tax That Failed

Congress needed money to pay soldiers and war debts, but the Articles gave it no power to collect taxes. It could only request money from the states, which often sent little or nothing. In 1781, Congress asked for the power to tax goods from other countries. Because changing the Articles required the approval of all thirteen states, Rhode Island's vote against the tax in 1782 was enough to defeat it.

What Historians Argue

Historians disagree about how to judge the Articles. In 1888, John Fiske named the 1780s "the critical period" and described a country close to collapse. In 1940, Merrill Jensen argued that the Articles did what their authors intended, which was to keep power in the states.

content.simplified:
In July 1776, the colonies had just declared independence. About a week later, John Dickinson of Pennsylvania gave the Continental Congress a plan for a national government. Dickinson had not signed the Declaration of Independence. He thought the break with Britain came too soon. Now that it had come, he wanted the thirteen states to stay together. His plan gave Congress more power than most states wanted to give.

Arguing Over Power

The delegates who read the plan had just gone to war against a king. For years, that king and Parliament had made laws for the colonies from across an ocean. Many delegates did not want a new government that could do the same thing. Most Americans also felt loyal to their own state first. A farmer in Virginia called Virginia his country. A merchant in Boston said the same about Massachusetts.

So Congress spent more than a year cutting the plan down. Thomas Burke of North Carolina warned that Congress would keep taking power away from the states if it could. In 1777, he proposed a rule that each state would keep its own power and independence. Eleven states voted for it. In November 1777, Congress approved the Articles of Confederation, the first written plan of government for the United States. Then it sent the plan to the states to approve.

A League of Friendship

The Articles created a confederation, a loose union of states that agree to work together but keep most of their own power. The plan called the union "a firm league of friendship." The states promised to defend one another and to follow the decisions of Congress. But Congress had no way to make a state keep that promise.

Under the Articles, Congress ran the country. There was no president to carry out laws, and there were no national courts. Each state sent delegates, but each state had only one vote. Virginia had more than ten times as many people as Delaware. Still, the two states counted the same. The large states would argue about this again in 1787.

Waiting for Maryland

The states were slow to approve the plan because they did not trust one another. Several large states, including Virginia, claimed land in the West. This land lay between the Appalachian Mountains and the Mississippi River, and many Native nations lived on it. Maryland had no land in the West. Its leaders feared that Virginia would grow rich by selling the land to settlers. So Maryland refused to sign until the large states gave their claims to Congress. Virginia finally agreed. On March 1, 1781, Maryland's delegates signed. The Articles went into effect while the war against Britain was still going on.

The Tax That Failed

Congress needed money. Soldiers had gone months without pay. The country owed money to France and to its own citizens. But the Articles did not let Congress collect taxes. It could only ask each state to send money, and the states often sent little or nothing. In 1781, Congress asked the states for the power to collect a tax of 5 percent on goods from other countries. That meant $5 on every $100 of goods. Almost every state agreed. But to change the Articles, all thirteen states had to vote yes. In November 1782, Rhode Island voted no. A month later, Virginia took back its approval, and the tax plan ended.

Why It Matters: The Articles of Confederation was the first government of the United States. The problems Congress faced under it led the states to send delegates to Philadelphia in 1787.

After the war, paper money from Congress was worth almost nothing. Massachusetts raised its taxes. People had to pay in gold or silver coins. Few farmers had coins. Courts took the farms of people who could not pay. In 1786, farmers with guns closed the courts.

It also banned slavery there. By then, Congress had asked the states to meet in Philadelphia to fix the Articles.

Four rebels were killed, and the rest scattered. American leaders disagreed about what the uprising meant. George Washington wrote in October 1786 that "Influence is no government." Thomas Jefferson wrote from Paris in January 1787 that "a little rebellion now and then is a good thing." In February, Congress invited the states to send delegates to Philadelphia to revise the Articles.

One Success

Congress did solve one problem that summer. In July 1787, it passed the Northwest Ordinance, a law that set up a government for the land north of the Ohio River and explained how parts of it could become new states. The law declared that "there shall be neither slavery nor involuntary servitude" in the territory. It also promised that the lands of Native nations "shall never be taken from them without their consent." Within a few years, the U.S. Army was fighting Native nations for that land.

Historians once described the rebels as poor farmers deep in debt. In 2002, Leonard Richards compared lists of the rebels with court records and found that many owed little. He argued that they were protesting a tax plan that favored the wealthy men who held the state's war debt.

content.simplified:
On a snowy day in January 1787, more than a thousand armed farmers marched toward the federal arsenal at Springfield, Massachusetts. An arsenal is a building where weapons are stored. This one held thousands of muskets. Many of the farmers had fought in the Revolution. Their leader, Daniel Shays, had been a captain in the Continental Army. The trouble that brought them to Springfield had started with money.

Money Nobody Trusted

During the war, Congress paid for soldiers and supplies by printing paper money called Continental dollars. It printed so many that each one lost almost all its value. People began to say that something useless was "not worth a Continental." After the war, many states printed their own paper money. Bills from one state often were not accepted in the next. A merchant could not be sure what the money in his hand was worth.

Trouble With Neighbors

The states also fought over trade. Some states taxed goods that came from other states, just as they taxed goods from Britain. Maryland and Virginia argued over who could fish and ship goods on the Potomac River, which ran between them. In 1785, leaders from the two states met at Mount Vernon, the home of George Washington. They settled the problem themselves. Congress played no part.

Other countries took advantage of the weak national government. British soldiers stayed in forts around the Great Lakes. Britain had agreed in the peace treaty to leave them. In 1784, Spain closed the port of New Orleans to American boats. Farmers west of the Appalachians needed the Mississippi River to ship their crops to market. Congress had no money for an army or navy, so it could not make either country back down.

Organizing the West

Congress did solve one big problem. It now controlled the land the states had given up. This land lay north of the Ohio River and east of the Mississippi. In 1785, Congress ordered workers to measure the land and divide it into square townships. Each township was six miles on a side. It had 36 sections of 640 acres each, and one section was set aside to pay for a public school.

In July 1787, Congress passed the Northwest Ordinance. This law set up a government for the region, which was called the Northwest Territory. When part of the territory had 5,000 free adult men, they could elect their own lawmakers. When it reached 60,000 people, it could ask to join the union as a new state, equal to the first thirteen. The law banned slavery in the territory. It also promised that the "lands and property" of Native nations "shall never be taken from them without their consent." Within a few years, settlers and the U.S. Army were fighting Native nations for that same land.

Shays' Rebellion

In Massachusetts, the state government owed money from the war. In 1786, lawmakers raised taxes and said people must pay in gold or silver coins. Few farmers had coins. When farmers could not pay their taxes or debts, courts took their farms. Some farmers went to jail. That summer and fall, armed farmers in western Massachusetts closed the courthouses so judges could not take any more land.

The march on Springfield was the next step. Congress could not help Massachusetts, because it had almost no army and no money to pay one. So Governor James Bowdoin raised a state militia, or citizen army. Boston merchants helped pay for it. On January 25, 1787, the militia fired cannons at Shays' men as they came near the arsenal. Four rebels were killed, and the rest ran. Shays escaped to Vermont and was later pardoned.

A Call to Philadelphia

Leaders in other states watched Massachusetts with alarm. Some had already been trying to fix the Articles. In September 1786, delegates from five states met at Annapolis, Maryland, to talk about trade. Too few states came to get anything done. But two delegates wrote a report calling for a larger meeting in Philadelphia the next May. They were Alexander Hamilton of New York and James Madison of Virginia. After Shays' Rebellion, Congress agreed. In February 1787, it invited every state to send delegates to Philadelphia to fix the Articles of Confederation.

Why It Matters: The Northwest Ordinance banned slavery north of the Ohio River, so the river became a dividing line between free and slave land. Shays' Rebellion helped convince twelve states to send delegates to Philadelphia.

James Madison of Virginia reached Philadelphia in early May 1787, more than a week before the meeting was scheduled to begin. While he waited for other delegates to arrive, he and the Virginians drafted a plan for a new national government.

Behind Closed Doors

A convention is a formal meeting held for a special purpose, and each state chose delegates, people sent to represent it. Congress had called this meeting "for the sole and express purpose of revising the Articles of Confederation." The Constitutional Convention opened on May 25 in the Pennsylvania State House, and the delegates elected George Washington to lead it. Over the summer, 55 delegates from twelve states took part, while Rhode Island refused to send anyone. The delegates agreed to keep their debates secret so they could argue freely. Madison wrote down nearly every speech, and his notes, first published in 1840, remain the main record of the debates.

Who Was Left Out

To be included means to be part of a group and have a voice in it, and to be excluded means to be kept out. All 55 delegates were white men, and most were wealthy. From Paris, Thomas Jefferson called the convention "an assembly of demigods." Women, enslaved people and Native nations had no one in the room. In 1790, nearly one in five people in the United States was enslaved, and in most states only men who owned property could vote.

What Historians Argue

In 1913, the historian Charles Beard argued that the delegates designed the new government to protect their own property. In 1958, Forrest McDonald examined the delegates' financial records and found that their votes did not follow their investments. Historians still disagree about how much the delegates' wealth shaped the Constitution.

James Madison of Virginia reached Philadelphia in early May 1787. He was more than a week early. He was 36 years old, short and quiet. He had spent the past year reading about governments in history. When May 14 came, only the delegates from Virginia and Pennsylvania had arrived. So Madison and the other Virginians met each day while they waited. Edmund Randolph spoke for most of the day on May 29, 1787. He listed the problems of the Articles of Confederation one by one. Then he laid out fifteen ideas that Madison and the other Virginians had written. Their plan did not fix the Articles. It replaced them with a new and much stronger national government.

The Virginia Plan

The Virginia Plan divided the national government into three branches. One branch would make laws. One would carry them out. One would act as the courts. The lawmaking branch is called the legislature. In this plan it would have two houses. A legislature with two houses is called bicameral, from Latin words that mean "two rooms."

The biggest change was in representation, the way people get a voice in government. Under the Articles, every state had one vote. Under the Virginia Plan, a state with more people would get more lawmakers in both houses. Virginia was the largest state. It would have about ten times as many votes as Delaware. Delegates from the large states liked this idea. Delegates from the small states saw it as a way for the large states to run the country.

The New Jersey Plan

On June 15, William Paterson of New Jersey offered a different plan. It kept a Congress with one house, where every state had one vote, as under the Articles. It gave Congress new powers. Congress could tax goods from other countries and control trade. Paterson said the states had sent the delegates to fix the Articles, not to throw them out. Four days later, most of the delegates voted against his plan.

A Summer Stuck in One Place

That vote did not end the fight. Through the hot weeks of late June and early July, the delegates argued about representation almost every day. On July 2, they voted on whether each state should have an equal vote in the second house. The vote was a tie. Five states voted yes, five voted no, and one state was split. Some delegates began to talk about going home. So the convention chose a committee, with one delegate from each state, to look for a middle path.

Meeting in the Middle

A compromise is an agreement in which each side gives up part of what it wants. Benjamin Franklin compared it to a carpenter fitting two boards whose edges do not match. The carpenter, he said, "takes a little from both, and makes a good joint." The committee started from an idea that Roger Sherman of Connecticut had been suggesting for weeks.

Under Sherman's plan, Congress would have two houses. In the House of Representatives, a state with more people would have more members. The people would be counted every ten years. Voters would elect House members every two years. In the Senate, every state would have two senators, no matter its size. Each state's legislature would choose them. The large states got their way in one house, and the small states got theirs in the other.

On July 16, 1787, the convention approved the plan by one vote. Five states voted yes and four voted no, with Massachusetts split. The plan became known as the Great Compromise. The next day, the delegates moved on to other questions.

Why It Matters: Congress still follows the Great Compromise. California has about 39 million people and 52 members in the House. Wyoming has fewer than 600,000 people and one member. Each state has two senators.

The delegates had agreed that seats in the House would depend on population. A harder question followed. They had to decide who would count as part of a state's population. The first national count, in 1790, found nearly 700,000 enslaved people in the United States. Nine out of ten of them lived in the South. The answer would decide how much power each region had in the new government.

Counting People for Power

Delegates from the South wanted enslaved people counted the same as free people. More people meant more seats in the House. Enslaved people could not vote. So the extra seats would go to the white men who held them in slavery. Delegates from the North objected. Southern law treated enslaved people as property. Northern delegates argued that property should not earn seats in Congress.

In 1783, Congress had used a ratio of three to five to divide war costs among the states. James Wilson of Pennsylvania suggested using the same ratio for representation. Under this rule, three out of every five enslaved people would be counted when seats in the House were divided. The same rule would be used for some taxes. In July, after more argument, the delegates accepted the Three-Fifths Compromise. The Constitution describes enslaved people only as "three fifths of all other Persons."

Trading in Human Beings

In August, the delegates turned to the slave trade. This was the business of bringing captured Africans to America by ship to be sold. Many delegates wanted Congress to have the power to end it. Luther Martin of Maryland argued that the trade went against the ideals of the Revolution. Delegates from South Carolina and Georgia said their states would never join a union that banned it.

Again the delegates compromised. The Constitution said Congress could not ban the slave trade before 1808. In return, southern delegates agreed to let Congress control trade with other countries by a simple majority vote. Congress did ban the slave trade starting January 1, 1808. By then, tens of thousands more Africans had been brought to the United States in chains.

Near the end of the summer, delegates from South Carolina added one more rule. If an enslaved person escaped to another state, that state had to return the person to the enslaver. Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, Connecticut and Rhode Island had laws or court rulings that were ending it step by step. Because of the fugitive slave clause, crossing into one of those states did not make an enslaved person free.

content.simplified:
In September 1787, a clerk named Jacob Shallus sat down with a quill pen and a stack of parchment. The delegates had paid him $30 to copy the final Constitution in his best handwriting. It took him about two days. The four pages he wrote are on display today at the National Archives in Washington, D.C. Because of the way they are organized, a reader can still find any rule in the Constitution in a few seconds.

A Plan in Seven Parts

After the Preamble, the Constitution is divided into seven articles. Each article is split into numbered sections. Some sections are split again into short paragraphs called clauses. A rule is named by where it sits. "Article I, Section 8" points to the list of powers given to Congress, the same way a street address points to a house.

The first three articles each create one part of the national government. Article I creates Congress. Article II creates the office of president. Article III creates the Supreme Court. The other four articles cover the rest. Article IV explains how the states treat one another. Article V explains how to change the Constitution. Article VI makes the Constitution the highest law in the country. Article VII explains how it would be approved.

An Idea From France

The delegates had read the work of a French writer named Montesquieu. In 1748, he argued that liberty is safest when no single person or group holds all the power of government. He described three kinds of power. One makes the laws. One carries them out. One judges whether the laws have been broken. When one ruler holds all three, Montesquieu wrote, nothing stops that ruler from becoming a tyrant. A tyrant is a ruler who uses power cruelly and unfairly.

The delegates built this idea into the Constitution. Dividing the work of government among three branches is called separation of powers. Each branch has its own job and its own people.

The Three Branches

The legislative branch makes the laws. Article I gives this power to Congress, which is made up of the House of Representatives and the Senate. Article I is the longest article. Its list of powers includes collecting taxes, coining money and declaring war.

The executive branch carries out the laws. To execute a law means to carry it out. Article II gives this power to the president. The president must be at least 35 years old and must have been born a citizen. The president serves a term of four years and also commands the army and navy.

The judicial branch decides what the laws mean and settles arguments over them in court. Article III creates the Supreme Court and lets Congress set up lower courts. Federal judges keep their jobs for life as long as they behave well. That way, they can decide cases without fearing that they will be fired.

When Shallus finished copying, the delegates checked his work against their notes. On September 17, 1787, they signed the four pages he had written.

content.simplified:
On June 1, 1787, James Wilson of Pennsylvania proposed that one person should lead the executive branch. Madison's notes record a long pause before anyone answered. Many delegates remembered King George III. They did not want to give that much power to anyone. Edmund Randolph of Virginia argued for three leaders, not one. In the end, the delegates agreed on a single president. Deciding how to choose that president took them most of the summer.

Three Ideas That Did Not Work

The Virginia Plan said Congress should choose the president. Many delegates worried that a president picked by Congress would always try to please Congress. Wilson and Gouverneur Morris wanted the voters to choose. Others argued that voters in 1787 had no way to learn about a candidate from a faraway state. News traveled by horse and ship.

A vote by the people raised one more problem. Enslaved people made up a large share of the population in the South, but they could not vote. Madison pointed out that in a direct election, the southern states would have fewer voters and less say. The third idea was to let state legislatures choose the president. It also failed. The delegates voted on these choices again and again and kept changing their minds.

The Electors

In early September, a committee offered a new plan. Each state would choose a group of people called electors. The electors would vote for president. Together, all the electors became known as the Electoral College. The word college here means a group of people with a shared job. It is not a school.

Each state gets as many electors as it has members of Congress. Washington state has 10 representatives and 2 senators, so it has 12 electors. The number of House seats depended on population, and population included three-fifths of enslaved people. So the plan kept the extra power the southern states had gained from the Three-Fifths Compromise. The Constitution let each state decide how to pick its electors. At first, many state legislatures picked them. Today, the voters in every state do.

How It Works Today

In an election for president, voters are choosing between groups of electors who have promised to support a candidate. In 48 states and Washington, D.C., the candidate who wins the most votes in the state wins all of its electors. Maine and Nebraska divide theirs. There are 538 electors in all. A candidate needs 270, which is a majority, to win.

Under this system, a candidate can win the most votes across the country and still lose. This has happened five times. The most recent time was 2016. The electors meet in each state's capital in December and cast their votes. On January 6, Congress counts the electoral votes and announces the winner.

Why It Matters: The Electoral College still decides every election for president. The number of electors a state has depends on its population, which is counted every ten years.

Some powers belong only to the national government, such as coining money, declaring war and making treaties. In 1788, Madison described these national powers as "few and defined" and the powers of the states as "numerous and indefinite." Powers not given to the national government are kept by the states. The Tenth Amendment, added in 1791, says they "are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people." These reserved powers include running schools and setting the rules for driver's licenses. Some powers, called concurrent powers, belong to both levels at once, such as collecting taxes and building roads.

What Historians Argue

Historians have asked where the idea of two levels of government came from. In 2010, Alison LaCroix argued that it grew out of the colonists' quarrel with Britain in the 1760s and 1770s. The colonists had claimed that Parliament could regulate trade for the whole empire but could not tax them, which meant dividing power between a central government and local ones.

James Madison came to Philadelphia with one idea he cared about more than almost any other. He wanted Congress to have the power to cancel any state law it disagreed with. Madison believed that state lawmakers had caused many of the country's problems. He thought only a strong national government could stop them. On July 17, 1787, the delegates voted on his idea. Seven states voted no, and only three voted yes.

Two Levels of Government

Most delegates did not want the states to disappear. They wanted a strong national government. But they also wanted the states to keep running much of daily life. So the Constitution set up two levels of government, national and state, and divided power between them. This system of sharing power is called federalism. The national government is also called the federal government.

In 1788, Madison explained the system to New York readers in a newspaper essay. The powers of the national government, he wrote, were "few and defined." The powers of the states were "numerous and indefinite." He meant that there were many of them and that they had no exact limits.

Who Does What

Some powers belong only to the national government. Article I gives Congress the power to coin money, declare war and set up post offices. Congress also controls trade between the states and with other countries. Only the national government can make treaties. These powers had caused trouble under the Articles, when each state printed its own money and taxed goods from its neighbors.

Other powers belong to the states. The Constitution does not list them. The Tenth Amendment, added in 1791, says that powers not given to the national government are kept by the states or the people. These are called reserved powers, because they are reserved, or held back, for the states. States run schools. They set the rules for driver's licenses and marriage. They create city and county governments. That is why the age to get a driver's license is different in Washington than in some other states.

Some powers belong to both levels at once. These shared powers are called concurrent powers, from a word that means "happening at the same time." Both the national government and the states can collect taxes, borrow money and build roads. Both can set up courts and make and enforce laws. A person living in Washington pays some taxes to the federal government and other taxes to the state.

When the Two Levels Disagree

The delegates knew the two levels would sometimes clash. They did not give Congress the power Madison wanted to cancel state laws. They wrote a different rule. The Constitution and national laws are the highest law in the country. When a state law conflicts with them, the national law wins. The courts decide whether a conflict exists. Chapter 4 explains this rule, called the Supremacy Clause.

Why It Matters: Americans still argue about where national power ends and state power begins. Many cases in the Supreme Court are about that line.

content.simplified:
In April 1792, President George Washington received a bill from Congress. It set the number of seats each state would have in the House of Representatives. Washington believed the bill broke the rules in the Constitution for dividing seats. So he sent it back to Congress without signing it. He added a letter that explained his reasons. It was the first time a president had ever rejected a law passed by Congress.

Each Branch Can Stop the Others

Separation of powers gave each branch its own job. But the delegates worried that one branch might still grow too strong and take over the others. So they gave each branch ways to limit, or check, the other two. This system is called checks and balances. Madison explained the idea in an essay in 1788. "Ambition must be made to counteract ambition," he wrote. Each branch would guard its own power and keep the others from taking too much.

The President Checks Congress

When Washington sent the bill back, he used a veto. A veto is the power of a president to reject a bill passed by Congress. Veto is Latin for "I forbid." A veto does not have to be final. Congress can still pass the bill into law if two-thirds of the members in both the House and the Senate vote for it again. This is called overriding a veto. It is hard to do, so it does not happen often. Congress did not override a veto until 1845, more than fifty years after Washington's first one.

Congress Checks the President and the Courts

Congress has several checks of its own. The president chooses judges for the federal courts, but the Senate must vote to approve them. The president makes treaties with other countries, but two-thirds of the Senate must approve each one. Only Congress can spend money. So a president cannot carry out a plan that Congress will not pay for.

Congress can also remove a president or a federal judge who commits serious crimes. First, the House votes on impeachment, a formal accusation against the official. Then the Senate holds a trial. If two-thirds of the senators vote guilty, the official is removed from office. Being impeached does not mean being removed. Andrew Johnson was impeached in 1868, and the Senate fell one vote short of removing him. No president has ever been removed by the Senate.

The Courts Check the Other Two

The last check came from a court case, not from the delegates. In 1803, in a case called Marbury v. Madison, Chief Justice John Marshall ruled that part of a law passed by Congress broke the Constitution. The Constitution is the highest law, he wrote, so a law that conflicts with it cannot stand. The power to decide whether a law or an action of government follows the Constitution is called judicial review. The Constitution does not name this power, but the Supreme Court has used it ever since.

Washington's veto in 1792 worked the way the delegates had planned. Congress did not override it. Congress wrote a new bill that fixed the problems the president had named, and Washington signed it a few days later.

Why It Matters: Checks and balances are often in the news. They appear when a president vetoes a bill, when the Senate votes on a judge, and when a court rules on whether a law follows the Constitution.

In the summer of 1790, more than two dozen Muscogee (Creek) leaders traveled hundreds of miles to New York City. They came from what is now Georgia and Alabama. New York was then the nation's capital. Their leader, Alexander McGillivray, had come to make a treaty with President George Washington. The Creek Nation and the state of Georgia had been fighting over land for years. McGillivray wanted the national government, not Georgia, to settle the matter.

Nations Before the United States

Native nations governed themselves long before Europeans arrived. They had their own leaders, laws and ways of making decisions. Many tribes in Washington state say their history on this land reaches back to time immemorial. That phrase means a time so long ago that no one can remember or measure it.

The power of a nation to govern itself is called sovereignty. European countries, and later the United States, dealt with Native nations as sovereign nations. They made treaties with them. These were the same kind of formal agreements they made with France or Spain.

A Problem Under the Articles

The Articles of Confederation gave Congress the power to deal with Native nations. But the Articles also said this power could not get in the way of a state's rights inside its own borders. No one agreed on what that meant. Georgia and New York made their own deals for Native land without Congress. In the 1780s, Georgia signed land treaties with a few Creek leaders. Most of the Creek Nation, led by McGillivray, said those leaders had no right to sign away land that belonged to all of them. Fighting broke out along the edge of Georgia.

What the Constitution Changed

The Constitution gave the national government clear control over dealings with Native nations. Article I, Section 8, gives Congress the power "to regulate Commerce with foreign Nations, and among the several States, and with the Indian Tribes." This is called the Commerce Clause. Commerce means trade and business. The clause names tribes next to foreign nations and states. In this way, the Constitution treated tribes as governments of their own.

Henry Knox was the secretary of war under President Washington. He was in charge of dealings with Native nations. Knox argued that the United States should buy Native land only through treaties that the tribes agreed to. It should not take land by force. In 1790, Congress passed a law. It said no one could buy land from a Native nation unless the national government approved.

That August, McGillivray and Washington signed the Treaty of New York. The Creek Nation gave up some of the land Georgia claimed. In return, the United States promised to protect the rest of the Creek Nation's land. The Senate approved the treaty, as the Constitution required.

Why It Matters: Since 2015, Washington law has required public schools to teach about tribal sovereignty and the history of the tribes in the state.

In December 1945, a 14-year-old Nisqually boy named Billy Frank Jr. was fishing for salmon on the Nisqually River, near what is now Olympia, Washington. State game wardens arrested him. Washington had laws that limited where, when and how people could fish. Frank and his family believed that a treaty signed ninety years earlier gave the Nisqually people the right to fish there. Over the next thirty years, he was arrested more than fifty times as he fought to prove it.

How Treaties Are Made

A treaty is a formal agreement between two or more nations. Under the Constitution, the president makes treaties, and two-thirds of the Senate must approve them. Between 1778 and 1871, the United States made about 370 treaties with Native nations. In most of them, tribes gave up some of their land. In return, the United States promised to protect the land the tribes kept. It also promised other rights, such as hunting and fishing.

The land a tribe kept for itself in a treaty is called a reservation. People often get this word wrong. The United States did not give reservations to tribes. The tribes reserved that land, which means they held on to it. It was part of the much larger territory they gave up.

Treaties in Washington

In 1854 and 1855, Isaac Stevens was the governor of Washington Territory. He made treaties with many of the tribes around Puget Sound and beyond. In the Treaty of Medicine Creek, the Nisqually and nearby tribes gave up most of their land. The 1855 Treaty of Point Elliott did the same for tribes from the Duwamish to the Snohomish, near where Seattle and Everett are today. These treaties promised that tribes could keep fishing "at all usual and accustomed grounds and stations." For the tribes, salmon were food, trade and a center of their culture. So this promise was one of the most important parts of the deal.

The Supremacy Clause

Washington's cities and fishing businesses grew, and the state passed its own fishing laws. Wardens arrested tribal members who fished in their usual places. The tribes argued that the state was breaking promises made in treaties.

The Constitution says what happens when a state law and a treaty conflict. Article VI says that the Constitution, the laws of the United States, and all treaties made by the United States are "the supreme Law of the Land." This rule is called the Supremacy Clause. When a state law conflicts with a treaty, the treaty wins. Every judge in every state must follow it.

In the 1960s, Billy Frank Jr. and other tribal members held "fish-ins." They fished in protest even when they knew they would be arrested. In 1970, the United States government sued the state of Washington on behalf of the tribes. In 1974, federal judge George Boldt ruled that the treaties still held. Treaty tribes had the right to catch up to half of the salmon that could be caught in their usual fishing places. Many fishermen and state officials fought the ruling for years. In 1979, the U.S. Supreme Court agreed with Boldt.

Why It Matters: The Boldt Decision still shapes how salmon are managed in Washington. Tribes and the state now manage the fish together.

content.simplified:
On September 12, 1787, the Constitution was almost finished. George Mason of Virginia rose to make one more proposal. Eleven years earlier, Mason had written the Virginia Declaration of Rights. It was a list of freedoms the state government could not take away. Now he asked the delegates to add a list like it to the Constitution. After nearly four months of work, the delegates voted no. Not a single state supported the idea. Five days later, Mason refused to sign the Constitution.

Nine States Needed

Mason was one of three delegates still in the room who would not sign. Edmund Randolph of Virginia and Elbridge Gerry of Massachusetts also refused. The other 39 signed. But the Constitution was only a proposal until the states agreed to it. To ratify means to formally approve. Article VII said special conventions in nine of the thirteen states had to ratify the Constitution. Then it would go into effect. Voters in each state would elect delegates to those conventions.

Newspapers printed the Constitution within days. Americans began arguing about it everywhere, in taverns, churches and town meetings. The people who supported the Constitution called themselves Federalists. The people who opposed it became known as Anti-Federalists.

The Federalists

The Federalists argued that the Articles had nearly ruined the country. They said a stronger national government was the only fix. In New York, the fight was close. There, Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay wrote 85 newspaper essays to defend the Constitution. They signed them all with the same made-up name, Publius, after a hero of ancient Rome. The essays were later collected as The Federalist Papers. They explained how separation of powers and checks and balances would keep the new government from misusing its power.

The Anti-Federalists

The Anti-Federalists were not against having a national government. They feared that this one was too strong. They worried that the president could become like a king. They worried that Congress would tax the people heavily and that the national courts would overpower the state courts. Mason wrote a list of his objections. The first one read, "There is no Declaration of Rights." Patrick Henry of Virginia made the same argument. So did Mercy Otis Warren of Massachusetts, who wrote under the name "A Columbian Patriot." Without a written list of rights, they said, nothing would stop the government from taking those rights away.

The Race to Nine

Delaware ratified first, on December 7, 1787. Every delegate there voted yes. Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Georgia and Connecticut soon followed. Massachusetts was harder. Many of its delegates were farmers who remembered Shays' Rebellion and did not trust faraway governments. The Federalists won them over with a promise. They would push for a bill of rights after the Constitution took effect. Massachusetts ratified by a vote of 187 to 168. Other states used the same promise.

On June 21, 1788, New Hampshire became the ninth state to ratify, and the Constitution became law. But the new government could hardly work without Virginia and New York, two of the largest states. On September 12, 1787, with the Constitution almost finished, George Mason of Virginia rose to make one more proposal. Eleven years earlier, Mason had written Virginia's Declaration of Rights, a list of freedoms the state government could not take away. Now he asked the delegates to add a similar list to the Constitution. After nearly four months of work, the delegates voted no. Not a single state supported the idea. Five days later, Mason refused to sign the Constitution.

Nine States Needed

Mason was one of three delegates still in the room who would not sign. Edmund Randolph of Virginia and Elbridge Gerry of Massachusetts also refused. The other 39 signed. But the Constitution was only a proposal until the states agreed to it. To ratify means to formally approve. Article VII said the Constitution would go into effect once special conventions in nine of the thirteen states ratified it. Voters in each state would elect delegates to those conventions.

Newspapers printed the Constitution within days, and Americans began arguing about it everywhere, in taverns, churches and town meetings. The people who supported the Constitution called themselves Federalists. The people who opposed it became known as Anti-Federalists.

The Federalists

The Federalists argued that the Articles had nearly ruined the country, and that a stronger national government was the only fix. In New York, where the fight was close, Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay wrote 85 newspaper essays defending the Constitution. They signed them all with the same made-up name, Publius, after a hero of ancient Rome. The essays, later collected as The Federalist Papers, explained how separation of powers and checks and balances would keep the new government from abusing its power.

The Anti-Federalists

The Anti-Federalists were not against having a national government. They feared that this one was too strong. They worried that the president could become like a king, that Congress would tax the people heavily, and that the national courts would overpower the state courts. Mason wrote a list of his objections. The first one read, "There is no Declaration of Rights." Patrick Henry of Virginia and Mercy Otis Warren of Massachusetts, who wrote under the name "A Columbian Patriot," made the same argument. Without a written list of rights, they said, nothing would stop the government from taking those rights away.

The Race to Nine

Delaware ratified first, on December 7, 1787, with every delegate voting yes. Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Georgia and Connecticut soon followed. Massachusetts was harder. Many of its delegates were farmers who remembered Shays' Rebellion and distrusted distant governments. The Federalists won them over by promising to push for a bill of rights after the Constitution took effect. Massachusetts ratified by a vote of 187 to 168. Other states used the same promise.

On June 21, 1788, New Hampshire became the ninth state to ratify, and the Constitution became law. But the new government could hardly work without Virginia and New York, two of the largest states. Virginia ratified four days later, by ten votes, and New York ratified in July by three. George Washington took the oath as the first president on April 30, 1789. Rhode Island, which had refused to send delegates to Philadelphia, ratified last, on May 29, 1790, by just two votes.

In 1982, Gregory Watson was a 19-year-old student at the University of Texas. He was looking for a topic for a government paper. In a library book, he found an amendment that James Madison had proposed in 1789. It said that when Congress voted itself a pay raise, the raise could not start until after the next election. Only a few states had ever approved it, but it had no deadline. Watson argued in his paper that it could still be added to the Constitution. His teacher gave him a C.

Why the Framers Allowed Change

The delegates in Philadelphia knew their plan was not perfect. They had seen what happened under the Articles of Confederation, when a single state could block any change. So they made it possible to change the Constitution, but not easy. A change to the Constitution is called an amendment.

Article V describes two steps. First, an amendment must be proposed. A proposal is a formal suggestion for a change. Two-thirds of the members of both the House and the Senate can propose an amendment. There is also a second way. Two-thirds of the state legislatures can ask Congress to call a national convention to propose one. That has never happened.

Second, three-fourths of the states must ratify the amendment. With 50 states today, that means 38 states must say yes. Under the Articles, one state could stop a change. Under the Constitution, it takes 13 states saying no.

Twenty-Seven Amendments

Members of Congress have proposed more than 11,000 amendments since 1789. Only 27 have been ratified. The first ten, the Bill of Rights, were added together in 1791. The others came one at a time over more than two hundred years.

An amendment does not erase words from the original Constitution. It is added at the end, and it can change or cancel an earlier rule. In 1919, the Eighteenth Amendment banned the sale of alcohol. The ban did not work as planned. In 1933, the Twenty-first Amendment repealed, or canceled, it. Both amendments are still printed in the Constitution today.

A Student's Campaign

After he got his grade, Watson began writing letters to state lawmakers across the country. He asked them to ratify the old amendment Madison had proposed. One state after another did. On May 7, 1992, Michigan became the 38th state to approve it. More than 202 years after Madison proposed it, it became the Twenty-seventh Amendment. In 2017, the University of Texas changed Watson's grade to an A.

Why It Matters: Americans still propose amendments every year. Any change to the Constitution must pass through the same two steps written in Article V.

content.simplified:
In December 1965, Mary Beth Tinker was a 13-year-old eighth grader in Des Moines, Iowa. She wore a black armband to school. She and a few other students wore the armbands to mourn the people killed in the Vietnam War and to call for a truce. The school district had banned armbands two days earlier. Tinker refused to take hers off, and she was suspended. Her family took the school district to court. They argued that the suspension broke her right to free speech. That right came from an amendment written almost two hundred years earlier.

Keeping a Promise

In Philadelphia, James Madison had argued that a list of rights was not needed. The Constitution gave the national government only certain powers, he said. So it had no power to take away people's rights. But during ratification, the Federalists had promised several states a bill of rights. In 1789, Madison ran for a seat in the first House of Representatives against James Monroe. Many voters in his district wanted those rights written down. Madison promised to work for them, and he won the seat.

On June 8, 1789, Madison stood up in the House and proposed a list of amendments. Congress debated them through the summer and sent twelve to the states. Ten were ratified by December 15, 1791. Together, these first ten amendments are called the Bill of Rights. Most of them protect individual rights. These are freedoms that belong to each person and that the government cannot take away.

The First Amendment

The First Amendment protects five freedoms. People may practice any religion or none, and the government may not set up an official church. People have freedom of speech, the right to say what they think without being punished by the government. They also have freedom of the press. They may gather peacefully in groups. They may petition the government, which means to ask it to change things.

Protections in the Law

The Second Amendment protects the right "to keep and bear arms." Americans disagree about how far that right reaches. In 2008, the Supreme Court ruled that it protects the right of a person to keep a handgun at home for self-defense. The Third Amendment says the government cannot force people to house soldiers in peacetime, as the British had done.

The Fourth Amendment protects people from unreasonable searches of their homes and belongings. In most cases, police need a warrant before they search a home. A warrant is a written order from a judge. To get one, police must show the judge a good reason to believe a crime took place.

The Fifth Amendment says no person can lose life, liberty or property "without due process of law." Due process means the government must follow fair rules and steps before it punishes anyone. A person accused of a crime cannot be forced to speak against himself or herself in court. The Sixth Amendment gives an accused person the right to a quick, public trial, a jury and a lawyer. The Seventh Amendment adds jury trials in many other cases. The Eighth Amendment bans "cruel and unusual punishments." The Ninth and Tenth Amendments say that people keep rights not listed, and that states keep powers not given to the national government.

The Schoolhouse Gate

The Tinker case reached the U.S. Supreme Court. On February 24, 1969, the justices ruled 7 to 2 that the school had broken the First Amendment rights of the students. The armbands were a quiet form of speech and had not disrupted classes. Justice Abe Fortas wrote that students do not "shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate." The Court also said that schools can limit speech that seriously disrupts learning.

Why It Matters: Every one of these rights has limits, and courts still decide where those limits fall. Cases about speech, searches and fair trials reach the Supreme Court every year.

On November 5, 1872, Susan B. Anthony voted for president in Rochester, New York. Two weeks later, she was arrested, because women were not allowed to vote. In speeches before her trial, she argued that the Constitution already included her. "It was we, the people, not we, the white male citizens, nor yet we, the male citizens; but we, the whole people, who formed this Union," she said.

After the Civil War

Three amendments followed the Civil War. The Thirteenth (1865) ended slavery. The Fourteenth (1868) made everyone born in the United States a citizen and promised "the equal protection of the laws." Most Native Americans were not counted as citizens until Congress passed a law in 1924.

More Voters

In 2019, the historian Eric Foner called the three amendments passed after the Civil War a "second founding." He argued that they changed the Constitution so much that they created a new one, in which the national government was responsible for protecting the rights of citizens against the states.
